491.quote_or_event: “Fight with your Self; why fight with external foes? He who conquers himself through himself, will obtain happiness. The five senses, anger, pride, delusion, and greed--difficult to conquer is one's self; but when that is conquered, everything is conquered.”
491.explanation: Nami tells Indra that the real enemy is within and is hard to defeat, and that victory there carries every other victory with it.
491.tie_back: The kural warns against attacking or belittling a foe before securing the right ground; Nami also treats the enemy as difficult and names the self as the only ground from which full victory can be won.
491.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.35-36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
491._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The theme of not underestimating a difficult enemy is shared; the military idea of besieging ground is changed into an inner contest, so the fit is loose.

492.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable; … (in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Saṃsâra.”
492.explanation: When Indra urges King Nami to build walls, gates and a moat, Nami replies with a fortress made of virtues, guarded threefold and impregnable.
492.tie_back: The kural says even the strong gain greatly by fighting from a fortress; Nami agrees that a fortress brings victory, but his fortress is faith and patience and his battle is against karma.
492.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.20-22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
492._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (ellipsis omits the bow-and-arrow clauses). Direct fortress-and-victory imagery, moved from war to the inner life.

493.quote_or_event: “As a tortoise draws its limbs into its own body, so a wise man should cover, as it were, his sins with his own meditation. He should draw in, as it were, his hands and feet, his mind and five organs of sense, the effect of his bad Karman, and every bad use of language.”
493.explanation: The Sutrakritanga uses the tortoise, weak in itself but safe inside its shell, as the model for the monk who guards himself through restraint.
493.tie_back: The kural says even the weak can win if they guard themselves well in a safe place; the tortoise image shows Jain self-protection, though the danger guarded against is karma, not an army.
493.source: Sutrakritanga I.8.16-17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
493._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It matches the idea of guarding oneself; the kural's aim of destroying the enemy has no Jain counterpart.

494.quote_or_event: “The Buddhas that were, and the Buddhas that will be, they (as it were) have Peace as their foundation, even as all things have the earth for their foundation. And if any accidents whatever befall him who has gained that (foundation), he will not be overpowered by them as a mountain by the storm.”
494.explanation: Here 'Buddhas' means the Tirthankaras; the sage who stands firmly on the ground of peace cannot be overpowered, as a mountain is not moved by a storm.
494.tie_back: The kural says that those who hold fast to their chosen ground defeat the plans of their enemies; the Jain sage who holds to the foundation of peace is similarly beyond the reach of every assault.
494.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.36-37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
494._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; Jacobi's footnote glosses 'Buddhas' as Tirthakaras. A good match on holding firm ground; the attackers here are misfortunes, not plotting enemies.

495.quote_or_event: Jain metaphysics holds that souls and matter can move only where dharmastikaya, the medium of motion, is present, and come to rest by means of adharmastikaya, the medium of rest. Commentators illustrate this with the fish, which moves freely only in water, the water being the medium of its movement.
495.explanation: In Jain cosmology the power to move depends on being in the right medium; outside that medium, motion is impossible however strong the being is.
495.tie_back: Valluvar's crocodile is mighty in deep water and helpless out of it; the Jain doctrine of the medium of motion, with its fish-in-water illustration, likewise makes a being's power depend on the element it is in.
495.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.17 of Umasvati (paraphrase), with the traditional fish-in-water illustration from the commentaries
495._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the sutra's teaching is standard, but the fish illustration is commentarial and its exact wording was not verified this session. A metaphysical parallel, not an ethical teaching about strategy.

496.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra teaches that a soul freed from all karma rises to the top of the inhabited universe (loka) and goes no further, because the medium of motion (dharmastikaya) does not exist beyond it. Even a perfected soul cannot move where its medium is absent.
496.explanation: Jainism holds that even the highest being's movement is limited by the medium available to it.
496.tie_back: The kural says the strong chariot cannot run on the sea nor the ship on land; Jain doctrine gives a cosmic version of the same rule, since no being, however perfect, can travel where its medium of motion is absent.
496._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutra; wording not quoted from any translation. The structural parallel is real, but the subject is cosmology, not choosing the right field of action.

497.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
497.explanation: The sage Gardabhali tells the frightened King Sanjaya, who had killed a deer in the monk's park, to be fearless and to grant fearlessness to all beings.
497.tie_back: The kural names fearlessness as the only ally a well-prepared person needs; Jainism also prizes fearlessness, but joins it to the gift of safety to others (abhaya-dana), whereas the kural is about attacking an enemy.
497.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 18.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
497._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. A shared value of fearlessness; the Jain verse joins it to non-violence, which runs against the kural's military aim.

498.quote_or_event: “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
498.explanation: Nami tells Indra that a single victory over oneself outweighs the conquest of countless warriors.
498.tie_back: The kural shows a small force standing on its own ground defeating a great army; Nami's saying likewise makes the single self, on its own ground, greater than thousands of foes, though Jainism moves the battle inward.
498.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
498._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Only the idea of the few or the one outweighing the many is shared; the kural's point about favourable terrain is absent.

499.quote_or_event: “Monks who equal the ocean in depth, who are difficult to overcome, are frightened by nobody (or nothing), and are not easily assailed, who are full of extensive learning and take care of themselves, will go to the highest place, after their Karman has been annihilated.”
499.explanation: The very learned monk, who has no fort or army, is described as hard to overcome and not easily attacked because of his depth and self-guarding.
499.tie_back: The kural says people without strong forts or special strength are still hard to beat on their home ground; the Jain monk too is unconquerable without walls, because his strength lies in himself.
499.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
499._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Matches being hard to overcome without fortifications; the kural's specific point about home territory is not present.

500.quote_or_event: “As an elephant, sinking down in a quagmire, sees the raised ground but does not get to the shore, so do we who long for sensual pleasures, not follow the path of monks.”
500.explanation: King Brahmadatta confesses that his attachment to pleasure leaves him like an elephant stuck in a bog, able to see firm ground but unable to reach it.
500.tie_back: The kural's mighty elephant becomes helpless once its feet sink in mud; the Jain text uses the same image of a powerful elephant stuck in a quagmire, here as a picture of the soul trapped by its desires.
500.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
500._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Striking match of image (great elephant made helpless by mire); the application is to bondage by pleasure, not battlefield terrain.

tattvartha-sutra-umasvati.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra of Umāsvāti (sutra content paraphrased; no specific translation quoted)
